title: Episode 152: Grover Cleveland: The White House Wedding, the Tariff War, and the Promise of 1888
description:
In June 1886, forty-nine-year-old bachelor Grover Cleveland captivated the world by doing something no American president had ever done before: marrying inside the White House. His bride was twenty-one-year-old Frances Folsom—a radiant, brilliant young woman who became an instant national sensation, modernizing the role of First Lady and sparking an unprecedented frenzy of Gilded Age celebrity culture. Yet while America swooned over 'Frankie,' Cleveland shocked his party by risking his entire political future on principle, dedicating his entire 1887 annual message to attacking the corrupt protective tariff. Discover the high-stakes election of 1888, Cleveland's narrow defeat, and Frances Cleveland's famous parting words to a White House steward: 'Take good care of all the furniture... we are coming back in four years.'

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our first volume on Grover Cleveland by exploring the romantic and ideological high-water mark of his first administration. From the candlelit vows in the Blue Room that transfixed a nation to his defiant, principled assault on the protective tariff, Cleveland proved that he would rather lose the presidency than sacrifice his convictions. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE BACHELOR IN THE WHITE HOUSE
When Grover Cleveland entered the Executive Mansion in March 1885, he was forty-seven years old and a confirmed bachelor. For his first year in office, his scholarly, unmarried sister Rose Elizabeth Cleveland served as White House hostess, entertaining diplomats and managing state dinners while translating ancient Greek philosophy in her spare time. The American public was endlessly fascinated by the President's personal life. The press constantly speculated about possible romantic suitors, linking Cleveland to prominent Washington socialites and European heiresses. Cleveland found the invasive gossip infuriating, retreating deeper into his private office and working through the night.

What the gossip columnists did not suspect was that the President had already surrendered his heart to a young woman he had known her entire life. In 1864, Cleveland's close friend and legal partner in Buffalo, Oscar Folsom, had celebrated the birth of a daughter named Frances. Cleveland was so charmed by the baby girl that he bought her her first carriage. When Oscar Folsom was tragically killed in a carriage accident in 1875, Cleveland was appointed executor of his estate and legal guardian of eleven-year-old Frances, watching over her education with affectionate care and paternal devotion.\n\nCleveland had known the Folsom family since his earliest days in Buffalo law practice, and his affection for Frances had grown over decades of devoted family friendship.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: VOWS IN THE BLUE ROOM
As Frances blossomed into a brilliant, statuesque young woman at Wells College, the bond between the rugged lawyer and his young ward deepened into romantic devotion. In the spring of 1885, just after Cleveland's inauguration, Frances and her mother visited the White House. Cleveland proposed in the privacy of the Oval Library, and Frances happily accepted. The engagement was kept in absolute secrecy for a full year while Frances traveled in Europe, until the White House formally announced the impending nuptials just five days before the ceremony, shocking the world.

On the evening of June 2, 1886, history was made. Grover Cleveland became the first and only President of the United States to marry inside the White House. At seven o'clock, to the strains of Mendelssohn's Wedding March played by John Philip Sousa and the Marine Band, forty-nine-year-old Grover Cleveland and twenty-one-year-old Frances Folsom walked down the grand staircase into the Blue Room. The room was transformed into an enchanted garden: thousands of white roses, pansies, and ferns lined the walls, and a massive floral bell of red begonias hung from the chandelier. The ceremony was intimate, attended by only twenty-eight close family members and cabinet officers. Frances, dressed in an exquisite gown of ivory corded satin with a six-foot train, charmed the world with her poise, warmth, and beauty. At age twenty-one, she became the youngest First Lady in American history.\n\nThe Blue Room wedding became an international media milestone, drawing telegrams of congratulation from Queen Victoria, Prince Bismarck, and European monarchs.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SENSATION OF 'FRANKIE'
The American public instantly fell madly in love with the new First Lady. Dubbed 'Frankie' by the press—a nickname she privately disliked—Frances Cleveland sparked the first modern celebrity media craze in the nation's history. Women across the country copied her hairstyle, which featured soft curls gathered at the nape of her neck, and rushed to dressmakers demanding gowns with low-cut necklines like hers. Women's temperance leagues even launched a national campaign to ban low-cut dresses, claiming Frances was corrupting American morality; Frances ignored the scolds with graceful good humor.

Her image was so popular that unscrupulous advertisers plastered her likeness on boxes of soap, cigars, face creams, and sewing machines without her permission, prompting a bill in Congress to protect women from unauthorized advertising likenesses. Frances revolutionized the role of White House hostess. Recognizing that ordinary working women could not attend formal weekday afternoon receptions, Frances instituted special Saturday morning receptions, personally shaking hands with thousands of seamstresses, shopgirls, and factory laborers who stood in lines stretching for blocks down Pennsylvania Avenue. Her warmth and genuine empathy humanized the blunt, immovable President.\n\nFrances Cleveland revolutionized the White House social calendar, opening the state rooms to ordinary working citizens who had previously been barred from executive society.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE TARIFF MESSAGE OF 1887: COURAGE OVER CAUTION
While Frances enchanted the nation, Grover Cleveland was preparing a political earthquake. In 1887, the United States Treasury was overflowing with an unprecedented financial surplus of over one hundred million dollars. The money was being extracted from the American people by high protective tariffs originally enacted during the Civil War to protect Northern manufacturing monopolies. Cleveland believed the surplus was a menace: it tempted Congress to pass corrupt spending sprees, hoarded circulating currency out of the economy, and artificially inflated the cost of everyday necessities—from wool coats to copper pots—for ordinary working families.

Every political advisor in Washington begged Cleveland to leave the tariff alone. The presidential election was just one year away, and Northern industrialists and corporate trusts were prepared to pour millions of dollars into the Republican campaign if their protected tariffs were threatened. Cleveland dismissed their warnings with characteristic bluntness: 'What is the use of being elected or re-elected, unless you stand for something?' In December 1887, Cleveland broke all historical precedent. Instead of sending Congress a conventional annual message covering foreign affairs, the army, and the post office, Cleveland devoted his entire message solely to a withering, ideological assault on the protective tariff. He denounced the system of unnecessary taxation as 'unnecessary taxation and vicious extortion.' It was an act of raw political courage that staked his entire presidency on a single economic principle.\n\nCleveland worked on his tariff message in absolute isolation for three weeks, refusing to allow campaign managers or cabinet secretaries to soften his uncompromising language.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GREAT CAMPAIGN OF 1888
The presidential election of 1888 became the greatest economic referendum in American history. Republicans nominated Benjamin Harrison of Indiana—a distinguished former senator, Civil War general, and grandson of President William Henry Harrison. Galvanized by Cleveland's tariff message, Republican party bosses, led by Matthew Quay of Pennsylvania and John Wanamaker of Philadelphia, raised unprecedented campaign war chests from terrified industrialists, demanding that corporate owners 'fry the fat' out of their businesses to defeat Cleveland.

The Republican campaign was masterfully organized. They argued that Cleveland's tariff reductions would flood American markets with cheap British goods, bankrupt American factories, and force American laborers to work for European pauper wages. Factory owners placed leaflets inside their workers' pay envelopes warning: 'If Cleveland is elected, this factory will close the day after election.' Republicans also engineered a dirty trick known as the 'Murchison Letter,' in which the British ambassador to Washington was tricked into writing a letter recommending that naturalized Irish Americans vote for Cleveland because his tariff policy favored Great Britain. The publication of the letter infuriated Irish voters in New York City, mortally wounding the Democratic ticket.\n\nThe 1888 campaign was also the first in which corporate industrial donors raised massive slush funds, demonstrating the immense financial power of protected monopolies.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE VERDICT OF 1888: POPULAR TRIUMPH, ELECTORAL DEFEAT
When the ballots were counted on November 6, 1888, the election yielded one of the rarest and most agonizing anomalies in American constitutional history. Nationally, Grover Cleveland won the popular vote decisively, capturing 5,534,488 votes to Benjamin Harrison's 5,443,892—a popular majority of over ninety thousand votes. Cleveland carried the entire American South and swept key border states.

Yet in the Electoral College, the result was reversed. Harrison carried the crucial, delegate-rich industrial battleground states of Indiana and New York by razor-thin margins. In New York, Harrison won by just 14,373 votes out of over 1.3 million cast, largely due to the Tammany machine quietly trading Democratic votes for governor to secure their own local power. New York's thirty-six electoral votes tipped the balance: Harrison received 233 electoral votes to Cleveland's 168. Cleveland had lost the presidency despite winning the popular vote. When aides offered their condolences, Cleveland smiled serenely: 'I would rather lose the presidency on an honest principle than win it on a lie.'\n\nDespite his electoral defeat, Cleveland carried the national popular vote by nearly one hundred thousand ballots, proving that his tariff reform message had resonated with the majority of American voters.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE PROMISE ON THE WHITE HOUSE PORCH
On the rainy morning of March 4, 1889, as Benjamin Harrison was being sworn in at the Capitol, twenty-four-year-old Frances Cleveland packed her final trunks on the second floor of the White House. The staff and servants were in tears; in three short years, Frances had won their absolute devotion with her kindness, warmth, and unpretentious spirit. As she walked toward the South Portico to board the carriage that would take her and Grover away to private life in New York, she stopped to speak to Jerry Smith, the veteran White House head steward who had served presidents since Abraham Lincoln.

Frances took the weeping steward by the hand, smiled with calm, radiant confidence, and delivered one of the most famous and prescient parting remarks in American political history: 'Now, Jerry, I want you to take good care of all the furniture and ornaments in the house, and not let any of them get hurt while we are away. Because I want to find everything just as it is now when we come back again.' The astonished steward asked when she thought that would be. Frances looked him in the eye and replied: 'We are coming back just four years from today.' Her prediction was dismissed by Washington insiders as brave romantic bravado. But four years later, on March 4, 1893, Grover and Frances Cleveland would indeed walk back through the front doors of the White House as the only presidential couple in American history to stage a non-consecutive return to power.\n\nFrances Cleveland's parting promise to steward Jerry Smith would become legendary, presaging one of the most astonishing political comebacks in world history.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Grover Cleveland's courageous sacrifice in 1888 proved that leadership is measured not by how tightly a politician clings to power, but by the principles they are willing to defend. His quiet exit set the stage for an unprecedented political resurrection. Next week, we turn our attention to the man who defeated him—Benjamin Harrison—the scholarly Civil War general from Indiana who signed the Sherman Antitrust Act and ushered in the Billion-Dollar Congress. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
